result:
A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the unpredictable timing of two or more processes touching the same resource, so the script works most of the time and occasionally corrupts or loses data. With a shared log file, the usual symptoms are interleaved or half-written lines, or entries that vanish because one writer overwrote another.

To avoid it, always append with `>>` (never `>`), and take a lock around the write with `flock` so only one process writes at a time:

```sh
{
  flock 9
  printf '%s %s\n' "$(date -Is)" "$msg"
} 9>>/var/log/myapp.log.lock
```

Redirect the block's stdout to the log file itself (`>>/var/log/myapp.log` after the `9>>...lock`), or put that redirect on the `printf`; the lock is released automatically when the block ends and file descriptor 9 closes.

`>>` alone is enough if every entry is a single short line written by one `printf`, because the kernel then seeks to the end and writes in one step. You need the lock as soon as an entry spans several commands or lines, or the script reads the file and then writes based on what it saw.

`flock` locks are advisory, so every writer must use the same lock file, and they are unreliable on some NFS mounts.
